Basis of the right: the Civil Code definition of ownership (the owner's right to enjoy and dispose of the thing) and the rule that no owner may be deprived of his property except as the law provides; the owner may claim his thing from whoever holds it without right (revendication).
Ground for damages: the general tort article of the Civil Code (any fault that causes harm to another obliges its author to compensate), and the rules on the fruits owed by a possessor in bad faith.

Element 1: the plaintiff's ownership of the property: an official deed (notarial, judicial or administrative) published at the land registry, or a livret foncier; check whether the property is registered and whether a private deed without fixed date can carry ownership of real property (it cannot, for transfers after 1971).

Element 2: the defendant's occupation of the property, its start date, and the absence of any contract or title (no lease, no loan for use, no sale promise, no co-ownership, no family right of residence).
Element 3 (for damages): the harm (loss of use, rental value) and its amount, usually fixed by an expert; the causal link with the occupation.
Burden of proof: the plaintiff proves ownership and the occupation; the defendant who claims a title must prove it (the one who alleges a release proves it).
Proof of the occupation: bailiff's report of findings (محضر معاينة), witnesses; occupation is a material fact provable by any means.

Competent section: the real-estate section (القسم العقاري) of the court of first instance; if the court has no such section, the civil section; listing before the wrong section is not a ground of inadmissibility but a referral.

Urgent route: eviction of an occupier without title is often asked of the summary judge (قاضي الاستعجال) when the lack of title is obvious and there is urgency; the summary judge cannot rule if there is a serious dispute on the merits (ownership contested).
Territorial jurisdiction: in real-property matters the court where the property lies; check whether this rule is of public order.

Exit to the administrative courts: if the State, a wilaya, a commune or a public administrative body is a party (as owner or occupier), the administrative court is competent under the organic criterion.
Exit to commercial courts: unlikely; check whether the occupied premises are business premises and the dispute is between traders.

Exit to the criminal judge: occupation by trespass (التعدي على الملكية العقارية) is an offence in the Penal Code; if a criminal case is pending on the same facts, the civil judge may stay (the criminal holds the civil in abeyance).

Limitation: the ownership action (revendication) does not prescribe by itself, but the defendant may raise acquisitive prescription (15 years of possession, or 10 with just title and good faith) as a defence.
Limitation of the damages claim: tort action prescribes 15 years from the harmful act; periodic sums (rental value) may prescribe 5 years; check which applies to occupation compensation.
Possessory actions (recovery of possession) have a one-year period from dispossession; they are a different action from the ownership-based eviction and should not be confused.
Who raises limitation: the debtor/defendant only, not the court of its own motion.

Formal notice (إعذار): not legally required before the eviction of an occupier without title; it is required before contractual damages, but not when the compensation arises from a harmful act; a notice by bailiff is nonetheless useful as proof of bad faith and of the start of fruits owed.
Bad faith of the possessor: the possessor in bad faith owes the fruits from the day he became in bad faith; a possessor in good faith keeps the fruits until the claim is filed.

Publication of the petition at the land registry: required when the claim seeks annulment, rescission, revocation or cancellation of published rights; probably not required for a pure eviction, but required if the claim also seeks to annul the defendant's deed.
Petition formal elements: court, parties' names and addresses, summary of facts and requests, supporting documents; fees paid; standing (the owner or his representative) and interest.
Required documents: ownership deed (published), certificate of non-appeal if title comes from a judgment, bailiff's report of occupation, notice if any, land registry certificate (شهادة عقارية).
Co-ownership boundary: a co-owner in indivision occupying the common property is not an occupier without title; the remedy is partition or compensation for exclusive use.

Lease boundary: a tenant whose lease expired or was rescinded is evicted under the lease rules (expulsion of tenant), not as an occupier without title; an oral lease or the receipt of rent may prove a lease.
Family boundary: a spouse or relative living in the marital home or the family dwelling may have a right of residence (custody housing); a divorced wife with custody may have a right to housing.
Heirs boundary: an heir occupying estate property is a co-owner, not an occupier without title.
Sale promise / buyer in possession boundary: a buyer under a private sale who is in possession has a contractual claim to defend; the dispute is about the validity of the sale.
Unregistered property / possession-based ownership: if the plaintiff only holds a possession certificate (شهادة حيازة) or private deed, his standing to evict may be contested.

Requests: eviction of the defendant and of anyone occupying through him; compensation for occupation; penalty payment (غرامة تهديدية) to enforce the eviction; costs; provisional execution where allowed.
Provisional execution: possible by law in some cases and at the judge's discretion in others; check the CPCM article.
Penalty payment: the judge may order a penalty payment to enforce an obligation to do (leave the premises).
Amendments: CPCM Law 08-09 of 2008 amended by Law 22-13 of 2022; the Civil Code amended by Law 05-10 of 2005 (article 124 reformulated).
Expert appointment: rental value / compensation commonly assessed by a court-appointed expert; the petition may ask for one.
